transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a bit hard to explain, really, but it's been weighing on me quite heavily lately. You see, I manage a fairly large engineering firm, and the days are just incredibly long and stressful, filled with endless meetings and blueprints and deadlines. By the time I get home, I'm just completely drained, both mentally and physically. And that's when it happens. What brings me in is that once I start eating at night—usually after my wife has gone to bed and the house is completely quiet—it feels like... like I'm watching myself from the outside. I can see myself sitting there in the kitchen, eating, and in my head, I'm practically screaming, telling myself to just stop, to put the fork down, to close the fridge. But it's like my body isn't listening to my brain anymore. My hands just keep going back for more, over and over, opening cabinets, unwrapping things. It's the most bizarre, terrifying feeling, being completely aware of what I'm doing but having absolutely zero ability to make myself stop doing it. I just... I feel so out of control, and it's starting to really scare me.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you start during these nighttime episodes?

Yes, exactly. Like I was just trying to say a moment ago, it’s... it is exactly that. I just absolutely cannot stop. It’s the most frustrating, humiliating thing because, you know, in my day-to-day life, I'm a manager. If there’s a problem with a structural load on a project, or a delay with the contractors, I step in, I make a decision, and I stop it. I'm the one in charge. 

But sitting there at my own kitchen island, at one or two in the morning, with just the refrigerator light buzzing... it’s like someone else has entirely taken the wheel. I'll be holding something, anything really, and my brain is going, 'You don't even want this, just put it back.' I can literally hear my own inner voice pleading with me. I'm watching myself do it. But my hands... they just keep moving, almost mechanically. It’s like a machine that’s been switched on and the off button is completely broken. I'll finish one thing, and before I've even swallowed, I'm reaching into the pantry for the next. It’s a total, complete inability to just halt the process, no matter how much I'm begging myself to.
Do you feel guilty or ashamed after these episodes of eating at night are over?

Guilty? Ashamed? Oh, doctor, those words don't even begin to cover it. It's... it's a crushing feeling, really. You see, after the whole thing is over, after I've finally stopped—usually because I physically can't fit another thing in my stomach, or because I'm terrified my wife is going to wake up and walk into the kitchen and see me like that—the reality of what I've just done comes crashing down on me. 

I look at the wrappers on the counter, the empty containers, the crumbs everywhere, and I just... I feel so incredibly pathetic. I mean, here I am, sixty years old, a man who runs a whole department, who tells engineers with master's degrees what to do all day, and I can't even manage my own eating. I clean it all up, of course, frantically wiping down the counters and burying the wrappers deep in the trash can so my wife won't see them in the morning. The secrecy of it all just adds to the shame. I'll go back up to bed, and I just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, feeling so bloated and sick, and my mind just races. I tell myself, 'You're disgusting, how could you do this again, you're weak.' It's a relentless loop of self-loathing. I just feel so ashamed of the lack of discipline, the sheer gluttony of it. It's like I have this dark, shameful secret life going on while everyone else is asleep, and the guilt of hiding it from my wife, of being this... this out-of-control person... it just eats away at me the entire next day.
Do you find that you're not very hungry during the day?

Well, it's... it's not quite like that, doctor. I wouldn't say I'm not hungry during the day. In fact, it's quite the opposite. I mean, my days, as I mentioned, they start early. I'm usually up by 5:30, checking emails before I even have my coffee. And by the time I get to the office, it's non-stop. I might grab a bagel or something quick if one of the junior engineers brings something in, but usually, I'm just running on caffeine and adrenaline until lunch. And then lunch... well, lunch is usually a working lunch, right at my desk, looking over CAD drawings or on a conference call. I'll have a sandwich, maybe a salad if I'm trying to be good, and I am hungry for it. I definitely feel the hunger. 

And then the afternoon drags on, more meetings, more putting out fires on job sites, and by 4:00 or 5:00, I'm absolutely starving again. I can feel my stomach rumbling during the late afternoon briefings. So, no, it's not a lack of hunger during the daylight hours at all. I eat normal meals, I feel normal hunger. It's just... it's just that the daytime eating feels completely different. It's functional, you know? Fueling the machine to get through the workday. But that nighttime thing... that's an entirely different beast. It has nothing to do with whether I ate enough at lunch or dinner. I could have a full steak dinner with my wife at 7:00 PM, feel completely stuffed, and still, by 1:00 AM, I'm back in that kitchen, tearing through the pantry like I haven't eaten in a week. So, yes, the hunger is there during the day, just like anyone else, I suppose. It's just that the nighttime eating doesn't seem to care what happened during the day at all.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over time due to these nighttime eating episodes?

Weight changes? You know, it's funny you ask that, because I've actually been thinking a lot about my weight lately, especially with everything that's been going on at night. But the truth is... I haven't really noticed any major shifts. I mean, I step on the scale in our master bathroom—it's one of those digital ones my wife bought last year, tracks everything on an app, though I don't use half the features—and the number is pretty much the same as it's been for the last, I don't know, five or ten years. 

I hover right around the same weight. Maybe I'll go up a pound or two after a particularly bad week of... of doing what I do in the kitchen at 2 AM, and maybe I'll drop a pound if I'm running around a job site all week in the heat, sweating through my hard hat. But significant changes? No, not really. And honestly, it baffles me. With the sheer volume of food I'm putting away in the middle of the night—the sleeves of crackers, the leftover pasta, the ice cream, whatever I can get my hands on—you'd think I'd be ballooning up. You'd think I'd need to go out and buy all new suits for work. 

But I don't. My pants still fit the same, my belts are on the same notch. It's almost like my body is just... processing it, or maybe I'm burning it off with all the stress at work, pacing the floor during conference calls. I don't know the science behind it. But no, the scale hasn't really budged in any meaningful way, which is a small mercy, I suppose, given the absolute chaos of my eating habits right now. It just stays right in that same familiar range, day in and day out, despite everything.
Do you ever feel like you're eating out of control during the day?

During the day? No, no, not at all. During the day, I'm the one calling the shots, doctor. I mean, I'm managing a whole department, I'm directing draftsmen and engineers, I'm on top of every schedule and material delivery for our projects. If I have a sandwich at my desk at noon, I eat the sandwich, I wipe my mouth, I throw the napkin away, and I go right back to looking at blueprints. There's no... there's no frenzy to it. I decide when I eat, what I eat, and exactly when I stop. It's completely rational, completely in my hands. 

But at night... see, that's exactly why I'm here talking to you. That's the whole crux of the problem. Because once the sun goes down, once everybody is asleep and I'm standing in that kitchen at one or two in the morning, it's like a switch flips and I am not the one driving anymore. 

It's the most bizarre, terrifying feeling, really. Once I start eating at night, it's almost like... like an out-of-body experience. I can literally see myself doing it. I'm standing there in the glow of the open refrigerator, and I'm watching my own hands reach into the bags, grabbing handfuls of whatever I can find—chips, bread, cold leftovers—and just shoving it into my mouth. And in my head, my rational brain, the guy who makes hundred-thousand-dollar decisions all day, is screaming, 'Stop! What are you doing? Put it down, go back to bed!' I am actively telling myself to stop, over and over again. But my hands... they just don't listen. They just keep going back for more, over and over, like they have a mind of their absolute own. It's like I'm just a passenger in my own body, watching this disaster unfold and being completely powerless to hit the brakes. So, during the day, I have all the control in the world. But at night... it's just gone. Completely gone.
Do you think that the stress from your work or other emotional factors might be triggering these nighttime eating episodes?

Stress? Emotional factors? You know, I've asked myself that very same question, doctor. I really have. I sit there in the dark, surrounded by empty wrappers, and I think, 'Why? Why am I doing this?' And naturally, you look for a reason, a cause. And work is the obvious culprit, isn't it? I mean, being an engineering manager, the buck stops with me. If a steel shipment is delayed, I'm the one on the phone with the supplier at 6 AM. If a junior guy messes up a load-bearing calculation, I'm the one who has to catch it before it goes to the client. The pressure is immense, it's constant. There's millions of dollars on the line, people's safety, the firm's reputation. It's a heavy load to carry, day in and day out. 

And then there's the usual stuff at home, you know, my wife and I getting older, worrying about retirement, the house needing a new roof—just life, just the regular emotional wear and tear of being a sixty-year-old man in this world. 

So, I try to connect the dots. I try to say, 'Okay, I had a terrible meeting with the zoning board today, so that's why I ate an entire loaf of bread tonight.' But... honestly? I can't. I just can't make that connection. Because there are days when everything goes perfectly. We win a big bid, the team is firing on all cylinders, I come home, have a nice dinner, watch a game, feel completely relaxed and content... and I still end up in the kitchen at 2 AM. And conversely, there are days when the sky is falling at work, I'm stressed to the absolute breaking point, my blood pressure is through the roof... and I sleep straight through the night without eating a thing. 

It just doesn't seem to follow a pattern. It's not like a math equation where stress equals nighttime eating. It feels entirely random. I wish I could say it was stress, I really do. It would give me something to blame, something to fix. If it was just stress, I could try, I don't know, meditation or playing more golf. But it doesn't feel like it's tied to my emotions or my workday at all. It just happens when it wants to happen, regardless of how I'm feeling when my head hits the pillow.
Do you ever feel like you're eating out of control during meals or snacks before bedtime?

Before bedtime? You mean like during dinner, or maybe having a little something while my wife and I watch the evening news? No, no, absolutely not. My evenings are, well, they're just like anyone else's, really. I get home from the office, usually around six or six-thirty, depending on how bad the traffic is on the interstate. We sit down, we have a normal meal, maybe some grilled chicken, some vegetables, nothing out of the ordinary. And if we are watching a ball game later on in the living room, sure, I might have a handful of pretzels or a piece of fruit. But it is just a normal snack. I eat it, I am done. I go into the bathroom, I brush my teeth, and I go to bed feeling completely fine. There is zero panic. Zero feeling of being out of control. 

But like I was trying to explain just a few minutes ago, what actually brings me in here, the whole reason I finally picked up the phone and made this appointment, is what happens after I go to sleep and wake back up. That is the only time it happens. Once I start eating at night, in the dead of the night, it is just exactly like I said. It feels like I can literally see myself doing it. I am standing there in the dark kitchen, and I am telling myself to stop, just begging myself to walk away, but my hands just keep going back for more. They open another cabinet, they tear into another box, completely ignoring my brain. So before bed? I am perfectly fine, perfectly normal, totally in the driver's seat. It is only when I wake up in the dark that the wheels just completely fall off the wagon.
Do you ever feel like you black out or lose consciousness while you're eating at night?

Black out? Lose consciousness? No, no, no. Honestly, doctor, sometimes I think it would almost be easier if I did. I mean, if I just woke up the next morning, walked into the kitchen, found a bunch of empty wrappers on the counter and thought, 'Gee, I must have sleepwalked,' well... maybe that would be less tormenting. At least I'd have an excuse. But no, I am wide awake. I am painfully, acutely awake for every single second of it. 

I feel the cold tile on my bare feet. I hear the hum of the refrigerator motor—it's an older model, makes this slight rattling sound when the compressor kicks on, I keep meaning to adjust the leveling legs on it. But I hear that hum. I feel the cold air hitting my face when I open the door. I taste every single thing I'm shoving into my mouth. 

Like I was saying before, I am fully conscious. My brain is completely switched on. I'm standing there, looking at the clock on the microwave—those bright green numbers, you know, 2:14 AM, 2:17 AM—and I'm literally doing the math in my head, calculating exactly how many hours and minutes of sleep I have left before my alarm goes off at 5:30 for work. I am fully aware of my surroundings, fully aware of what I'm doing. It's just that the... the mechanical linkage, if you will, between my brain screaming 'stop' and my hands actually stopping is completely severed. 

I remember every agonizing minute of it. I remember the exact sequence of what I ate, I remember the shame I feel while I'm standing there chewing in the dark. So, no, there's absolutely no blacking out. There's no losing consciousness, no amnesia, nothing like that. I am a hundred percent present for the whole miserable event, right from the moment I get out of bed to the moment I'm staring at the mess on the counter, just completely disgusted with myself.
Do you ever find yourself eating at night without remembering waking up to do so?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago about the blacking out, it’s really the exact same thing with waking up. I remember all of it. Every single time. It’s not like I just magically teleport from my pillow to the pantry, you know? I don't ever just 'come to' with a mouthful of food and wonder how I got there. I wish I did! But no, the waking up part is... well, it's actually one of the worst parts of the whole ordeal, to be honest. 

I'll be dead asleep, just completely out, and then... bam. My eyes just snap open. I’m staring straight up at the ceiling. We have this awful old popcorn texture on the ceiling in the master bedroom—my wife has been begging me to scrape it off for five years now, but anyway—I just lie there staring at it in the pitch black. And I know exactly what's happening. I lie there for maybe ten, fifteen minutes, just fighting it. I tell myself, 'Don't do it, just go back to sleep, turn over.' I pull the duvet up tight, I try to focus on my breathing, try to think about the project schedule for the new commercial park we're bidding on, anything to distract myself. 

But the urge just builds and builds. It's like a pressure valve that's stuck closed. Eventually, I'm the one who throws the blankets off. I remember swinging my legs over the side of the mattress. I remember my knees popping when I stand up—old high school football injury, they always pop when it's cold. I remember walking past my wife's side of the bed, trying to tread lightly so I don't wake her, making sure to step entirely over that one spot on the hardwood hallway floor that I know always squeaks. 

So, no, I never forget waking up. I am painfully aware of the exact moment I wake up, that whole miserable internal debate I have with myself while I'm still under the covers, and every single step I take down the hallway to get to the kitchen. There's no sleepwalking involved at all.
Do you feel any specific emotion right before you start eating at night?

Emotion? Right before? Well, no, not really. I mean, not one specific thing I could put a name to, like being sad or angry or stressed about work. It's not like I'm lying there in bed thinking about the zoning permits we're waiting on for that commercial park and feeling anxious, and then I go eat because of that. It's nothing like that at all. 

It's more just... a drive. A physical compulsion, almost. Like I was describing with the waking up part—I'm just lying there, staring at that popcorn ceiling, and it's just this overwhelming urge that I *have* to go to the kitchen. It's like an itch you can't scratch, or like when you're incredibly thirsty and all you can think about is a glass of water, except it's not thirst or even real hunger. It's just this intense, building pressure. 

I guess you could say I feel frustrated while I'm fighting it. You know, when I'm pulling the duvet up and trying to force myself back to sleep, I'm definitely feeling frustrated with myself because I know exactly what's about to happen and I hate it. I'm dreading it. But the actual trigger? The thing that makes me throw the covers off? It's not an emotion. It's just that the pressure gets too high, the urge gets too strong, and I just give in. I just can't fight it anymore. So, no, no specific emotion driving it, just that awful, unstoppable urge.
Do you ever feel like you're eating out of control during the day, even if it's just for a moment?

During the day? No, no, during the day I'm fine. I'm completely in control during the day. I mean, I'm at the office, I'm dealing with contractors, reviewing blueprints, managing my team—I'm a busy guy, I don't have time to sit around and eat, let alone lose control over it. My lunches are usually just a quick sandwich at my desk or a salad if I'm trying to be good, you know? I eat like a normal person when the sun is up. 

But at night... that's the whole reason I'm here, doctor. That's what brings me in. It's the night time. Like I was saying before about being fully awake and aware? It's like... it's like I'm standing outside of my own body, watching myself do it. I can see myself standing there in the kitchen, bathed in that awful yellow light from the fridge, and I am literally screaming at myself in my head. I'm telling myself, 'Stop. Just stop right now. Put the bread down, close the jar, just go back to bed.' I am commanding myself to stop. 

But my hands... it's like they have a mind of their own. They just keep moving. They just keep going back for more, opening another package, reaching for another handful. I'm watching my own hands betray me. It's the most bizarre, terrifying feeling, being completely aware, completely rational in your head, but physically unable to make your body obey your own commands. So, during the day, absolutely not. But at night, once I start... that's exactly it. That's the loss of control I'm talking about. I just can't make my hands stop.
Do you ever find yourself eating at night without first waking up and getting out of bed?

Without waking up and getting out of bed? You mean, like, keeping snacks on the nightstand or eating under the covers while I'm still half asleep? No, absolutely not. 

First of all, my wife, Susan, she would absolutely kill me if I brought food into the bed. She just bought these incredibly expensive Egyptian cotton sheets—thread count in the thousands, cost a small fortune, honestly I don't see the difference but she loves them—and she is exceptionally particular about keeping them pristine. 

But even besides that, no, it always involves getting up. Like I was telling you before about staring at that popcorn ceiling and the squeaky floorboard in the hallway, it's a whole... process. I don't ever just roll over and start eating. I am fully, painfully awake, and I have to physically get out of that bed. I have to swing my legs over, feel that familiar pop in my bad knee, and walk all the way down the hall to the kitchen. 

The kitchen is where it happens. It's never in the bedroom. I don't stash food in the dresser drawers, I don't wake up with cracker crumbs stuck to my back or wrappers in the blankets. It's always this deliberate, agonizing march down to the fridge. I mean, I suppose if I just kept a granola bar by the bed maybe it wouldn't be such a massive ordeal, but that's just not how this works for me. The urge specifically drives me out of the room. I have to get up, leave the sanctuary of the bedroom, and go down to the kitchen... it's almost like this miserable little pilgrimage I have to make every time. So, no, I never eat without actually getting up and leaving the bed first.
Do you ever feel guilty or ashamed after eating during the day?

During the day? Guilty or ashamed? No, no, not at all. Like I was saying, during the day, I'm completely fine. I mean, my daytime eating is just... normal. Boring, even. I'll grab a coffee in the morning, maybe a bagel if there's a breakfast meeting—we just had this huge sit-down with the city planners on Tuesday and someone brought in these incredible bagels from that place downtown, the one with the line always out the door, but I just had half of an everything bagel with a little cream cheese. Just normal stuff. 

And lunch is usually just a quick sandwich while I'm looking over CAD drawings or dealing with emails. Sometimes I'll go out with some of the junior engineers to the deli across the street from the firm, but I just order a turkey club or a Cobb salad. I don't overdo it. I don't sit there stuffing my face or eating in secret. I just eat to fuel up and get back to work. There's nothing to feel guilty about because I'm not doing anything wrong. I'm not losing control. 

The guilt... oh, the guilt is entirely reserved for the morning after. That's when it hits me. When I wake up and I see the wrappers in the trash, or I realize I ate half a loaf of bread and a whole block of cheddar cheese at 3 AM... that's when the shame is just crushing. I'll be standing in the shower before work, letting the hot water hit my back, just replaying what I did the night before, and I feel so disgusted with myself. I'm a grown man, a manager, I make decisions that affect millions of dollars in construction, and I can't even stop myself from eating a sleeve of crackers in the middle of the night. That's where the shame is. But during the day? When the sun is shining and I'm at the office? No, I don't feel any guilt about my eating then. It's strictly a nighttime problem, and a morning-after hangover of regret.
Do you ever find yourself eating at night without feeling a strong urge to do so beforehand?

An urge? Like, do I just wander in there and start eating for no reason? No, no, it's never like that. The urge is... it's the whole reason I wake up. It's not like I wake up because I have to use the restroom, or because the dog barked, or because I'm just restless, and then I think, 'Oh, well, since I'm up, maybe I'll have a snack.' It doesn't work that way. 

The urge is what pulls me out of sleep. It's like this... this gnawing, pulling sensation. It starts before my eyes are even open. I'll be dead asleep, dreaming about work or whatever—I have these recurring dreams where I'm trying to read a set of blueprints but the lines keep moving around on the paper, very stressful—but anyway, I'll be asleep, and then this feeling just starts creeping in. It's this overwhelming, undeniable compulsion that I have to eat. 

It's so strong, doctor. It's not a suggestion. It's a demand. Like I said before about lying there, staring at the ceiling, listening to the house settle? I'm lying there fighting the urge. I'm trying to ignore it. I'll try to focus on the ceiling fan, or I'll try to count backwards from a hundred, or I'll think about the concrete pour we have scheduled for the next morning. I try everything to distract myself from it. But the urge just gets louder and louder until it's all I can hear. It's like a physical pressure in my chest. 

So, no, I never just find myself eating without that urge. The urge is the catalyst for the entire miserable routine. If I didn't feel that urge, I would just sleep through the night like a normal sixty-year-old man. I wouldn't be making that agonizing walk down the hall, I wouldn't be standing in the fridge light, and I certainly wouldn't be sitting here in your office trying to explain why I can't stop eating crackers at three in the morning. The urge is always there first, and it's incredibly strong.
Do you think your nighttime eating episodes are triggered by a specific emotional state, such as anxiety or depression?

Anxiety or depression? Triggering it? You know... I've thought about that. I really have. Susan, my wife, she's always reading these psychology articles online, trying to figure me out. She's convinced it's stress from the firm. And, sure, my job is stressful. When you're managing engineering projects, the buck stops with you. If a structural support is calculated wrong, or if a contractor uses subpar materials to cut costs—which happened on that commercial build out on Route 9 last year, an absolute nightmare of a situation—it all comes back to me. So yes, I have anxiety. I worry about deadlines, I worry about budgets, I worry about whether the guys on the site are actually following the safety protocols. 

But... is that what triggers the eating? I really don't think so. I mean, I've had stressful days, days where I come home and my stomach is tied in knots because we're behind schedule and the client is breathing down my neck. And on those nights, sometimes I sleep like a baby. I just crash. And then there are other days, days where everything goes perfectly. The weather cooperates for a pour, the inspections pass with flying colors, we come in under budget—a rare thing, let me tell you, but it happens. I come home feeling great, relaxed, maybe Susan and I will watch a movie or sit out on the patio with a glass of iced tea. I go to bed feeling completely fine, not depressed, not anxious, just... content. 

And then, boom. 3 AM rolls around, and there's that urge. That same pulling, gnawing feeling dragging me out of bed and down the hall. It doesn't seem to matter what kind of mood I'm in when my head hits the pillow. Stressed, happy, sad, bored... the urge doesn't care. It just shows up anyway. So, I don't think it's tied to an emotional state. It feels entirely separate from my emotions. It's almost like it's on its own schedule, completely ignoring whatever is going on in my actual life or in my head during the day. It's just this mechanical, physical drive that kicks in, regardless of whether I'm having a panic attack about a blueprint or if I'm the happiest guy in the world. So, no, I wouldn't say anxiety or depression triggers it at all. It's just... it just happens.
Do you ever feel like you're unable to stop eating during regular meals or snacks during the day?

During the day? No, no, not at all. Like I was saying earlier about the deli and the lunches, I have absolute control when the sun is up. If I'm eating a sandwich while looking over the site plans, I can eat half of it, wrap the rest in foil, and stick it in the mini-fridge in my office for later. I can stop whenever I want. The day is fine. I'm the boss of myself during the day, just like I'm the boss on the job site. 

But... what brings me in here, what really drove me to finally make this appointment and sit in that chair, is what happens at night. Because at night, that control is just... it's completely gone. Evaporated. Once I start eating at night, it's the most bizarre, terrifying thing. It feels like I can see myself doing it, almost like I'm floating outside my own body or watching myself on one of the site security cameras. I'll be standing there at the kitchen counter in the dark, and my brain is fully awake, telling myself to stop. I'm literally thinking, "Put the box down. Close the fridge. Go back to bed, you're going to regret this." I am practically screaming at myself on the inside to just stop. 

But my hands... they just ignore me. They just keep going back for more. It's like they have a mind of their own, completely disconnected from the steering wheel, so to speak. I'll watch my own hand reach into a bag of chips or a box of cookies, pull out a handful, and bring it to my mouth, and I'm chewing and swallowing while actively telling myself to stop doing it. It makes absolutely no sense, doctor. I manage complex engineering projects, I direct crews of fifty men, I am in charge all day long. But at 3 AM, I can't even stop my own hand from reaching for another bite. I just stand there, watching myself do it, completely unable to hit the brakes. That's the loss of control that scares me.
Do you have any trouble sleeping or experience any unusual sleep patterns outside of these nighttime eating episodes?

Trouble sleeping otherwise? No... no, I really don't. And I know that sounds strange, considering everything I just told you about roaming the halls at three in the morning, but it's the truth. If it weren't for that overwhelming urge to eat, I would be a champion sleeper. 

I've always been one of those guys who can just hit the pillow and be out in five minutes. Susan, my wife, she absolutely hates it. She has to read her Kindle for an hour, she needs the ceiling fan on a specific speed, she even bought one of those little machines that plays the sound of ocean waves—the whole nine yards just to drift off. But me? After a twelve-hour day on a site, managing crews, dealing with the noise and the dirt and the constant, endless problem-solving... I mean, by the time I get home, I am just bone-tired. Physically and mentally drained. 

I usually get into bed around ten o'clock. We'll watch a little bit of the local news, mostly just so I can catch the extended weather forecast—because weather is everything in my line of work, you know? If we're scheduled to pour foundation and there's a heavy rain coming in, it can set the whole project back thousands of dollars, completely wreck my timeline. So I check the weather, I turn off the lamp, and I am out cold. I don't toss and turn. I don't lie there worrying about the mortgage. I don't have insomnia or wake up gasping for air or anything like that. 

The only time my sleep is ever broken, the *only* blip on the radar, is when that urge hits me. If that didn't happen, I'd sleep like a rock straight through until my alarm goes off at 5:30 AM. And the strangest part is, even after I... well, after I go to the kitchen and eat, once I finally go back to bed, I usually fall right back asleep almost instantly. It's like a switch just flips back off. So, no, outside of those trips to the kitchen, my sleep is perfectly normal. Heavy, deep, uninterrupted sleep.
Do you have any history of sleep disorders, such as sleepwalking or restless leg syndrome?

Sleepwalking? No, no, nothing like that. Like I was saying before, when I'm asleep, I am just... I'm out. Dead to the world. I don't wander around the house in my sleep. And Susan, she would absolutely know if I did. I mean, I told you about her ocean wave machine and the Kindle, right? She is such a light sleeper that if I even roll over too heavily, she sighs and shifts around. If I were actually sleepwalking, you know, getting out of bed while unconscious, she'd have had me at a specialist for that years ago. She reads all those medical articles online, remember? She'd probably try to diagnose me herself before we even got to the clinic. 

But no, when I get up and go down the hall to the kitchen, I am wide awake. That's the whole problem, really, I'm totally aware of what I'm doing, just unable to stop it. And restless leg syndrome? No, I don't have that either. I mean, my legs get sore, sure. That's where the shame is. But during the day? When the sun is shining and I'm at the office? No, I don't feel any guilt about my eating then. It's strictly a nighttime problem, and a morning-after hangover of regret.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any episodes of eating at night that are not preceded by a strong urge to eat
doctor.question: Do you ever find yourself eating at night without feeling a strong urge to do so beforehand?

target_item.reason: The doctor's question is asking about the presence of a strong urge or desire to eat before the nighttime eating episodes (a criterion for Night Eating Syndrome). My symptom profile covers Bulimia Nervosa symptoms (loss of control, eating large amounts, compensatory behaviors, body image disturbance), but does not contain a specific item for having a strong urge to eat at night.

patient.answer:
An urge? Like, do I just wander in there and start eating for no reason? No, no, it's never like that. The urge is... it's the whole reason I wake up. It's not like I wake up because I have to use the restroom, or because the dog barked, or because I'm just restless, and then I think, 'Oh, well, since I'm up, maybe I'll have a snack.' It doesn't work that way. 

The urge is what pulls me out of sleep. It's like this... this gnawing, pulling sensation. It starts before my eyes are even open. I'll be dead asleep, dreaming about work or whatever—I have these recurring dreams where I'm trying to read a set of blueprints but the lines keep moving around on the paper, very stressful—but anyway, I'll be asleep, and then this feeling just starts creeping in. It's this overwhelming, undeniable compulsion that I have to eat. 

It's so strong, doctor. It's not a suggestion. It's a demand. Like I said before about lying there, staring at the ceiling, listening to the house settle? I'm lying there fighting the urge. I'm trying to ignore it. I'll try to focus on the ceiling fan, or I'll try to count backwards from a hundred, or I'll think about the concrete pour we have scheduled for the next morning. I try everything to distract myself from it. But the urge just gets louder and louder until it's all I can hear. It's like a physical pressure in my chest. 

So, no, I never just find myself eating without that urge. The urge is the catalyst for the entire miserable routine. If I didn't feel that urge, I would just sleep through the night like a normal sixty-year-old man. I wouldn't be making that agonizing walk down the hall, I wouldn't be standing in the fridge light, and I certainly wouldn't be sitting here in your office trying to explain why I can't stop eating crackers at three in the morning. The urge is always there first, and it's incredibly strong.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's nighttime eating is related to a specific emotional state
doctor.question: Do you think your nighttime eating episodes are triggered by a specific emotional state, such as anxiety or depression?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional triggers for the nighttime eating episodes, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Anxiety or depression? Triggering it? You know... I've thought about that. I really have. Susan, my wife, she's always reading these psychology articles online, trying to figure me out. She's convinced it's stress from the firm. And, sure, my job is stressful. When you're managing engineering projects, the buck stops with you. If a structural support is calculated wrong, or if a contractor uses subpar materials to cut costs—which happened on that commercial build out on Route 9 last year, an absolute nightmare of a situation—it all comes back to me. So yes, I have anxiety. I worry about deadlines, I worry about budgets, I worry about whether the guys on the site are actually following the safety protocols. 

But... is that what triggers the eating? I really don't think so. I mean, I've had stressful days, days where I come home and my stomach is tied in knots because we're behind schedule and the client is breathing down my neck. And on those nights, sometimes I sleep like a baby. I just crash. And then there are other days, days where everything goes perfectly. The weather cooperates for a pour, the inspections pass with flying colors, we come in under budget—a rare thing, let me tell you, but it happens. I come home feeling great, relaxed, maybe Susan and I will watch a movie or sit out on the patio with a glass of iced tea. I go to bed feeling completely fine, not depressed, not anxious, just... content. 

And then, boom. 3 AM rolls around, and there's that urge. That same pulling, gnawing feeling dragging me out of bed and down the hall. It doesn't seem to matter what kind of mood I'm in when my head hits the pillow. Stressed, happy, sad, bored... the urge doesn't care. It just shows up anyway. So, I don't think it's tied to an emotional state. It feels entirely separate from my emotions. It's almost like it's on its own schedule, completely ignoring whatever is going on in my actual life or in my head during the day. It's just this mechanical, physical drive that kicks in, regardless of whether I'm having a panic attack about a blueprint or if I'm the happiest guy in the world. So, no, I wouldn't say anxiety or depression triggers it at all. It's just... it just happens.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's nighttime eating episodes are related to a lack of control over eating in general
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you're unable to stop eating during regular meals or snacks during the day?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that once I start eating at night, it feels like I can see myself doing it and telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about feeling unable to stop eating during regular meals or snacks directly asks about a sense of lack of control over eating.

patient.answer:
During the day? No, no, not at all. Like I was saying earlier about the deli and the lunches, I have absolute control when the sun is up. If I'm eating a sandwich while looking over the site plans, I can eat half of it, wrap the rest in foil, and stick it in the mini-fridge in my office for later. I can stop whenever I want. The day is fine. I'm the boss of myself during the day, just like I'm the boss on the job site. 

But... what brings me in here, what really drove me to finally make this appointment and sit in that chair, is what happens at night. Because at night, that control is just... it's completely gone. Evaporated. Once I start eating at night, it's the most bizarre, terrifying thing. It feels like I can see myself doing it, almost like I'm floating outside my own body or watching myself on one of the site security cameras. I'll be standing there at the kitchen counter in the dark, and my brain is fully awake, telling myself to stop. I'm literally thinking, "Put the box down. Close the fridge. Go back to bed, you're going to regret this." I am practically screaming at myself on the inside to just stop. 

But my hands... they just ignore me. They just keep going back for more. It's like they have a mind of their own, completely disconnected from the steering wheel, so to speak. I'll watch my own hand reach into a bag of chips or a box of cookies, pull out a handful, and bring it to my mouth, and I'm chewing and swallowing while actively telling myself to stop doing it. It makes absolutely no sense, doctor. I manage complex engineering projects, I direct crews of fifty men, I am in charge all day long. But at 3 AM, I can't even stop my own hand from reaching for another bite. I just stand there, watching myself do it, completely unable to hit the brakes. That's the loss of control that scares me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's nighttime eating episodes are related to a sleep disorder
doctor.question: Do you have any trouble sleeping or experience any unusual sleep patterns outside of these nighttime eating episodes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sleep issues or unusual sleep patterns outside of the eating episodes, which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Trouble sleeping otherwise? No... no, I really don't. And I know that sounds strange, considering everything I just told you about roaming the halls at three in the morning, but it's the truth. If it weren't for that overwhelming urge to eat, I would be a champion sleeper. 

I've always been one of those guys who can just hit the pillow and be out in five minutes. Susan, my wife, she absolutely hates it. She has to read her Kindle for an hour, she needs the ceiling fan on a specific speed, she even bought one of those little machines that plays the sound of ocean waves—the whole nine yards just to drift off. But me? After a twelve-hour day on a site, managing crews, dealing with the noise and the dirt and the constant, endless problem-solving... I mean, by the time I get home, I am just bone-tired. Physically and mentally drained. 

I usually get into bed around ten o'clock. We'll watch a little bit of the local news, mostly just so I can catch the extended weather forecast—because weather is everything in my line of work, you know? If we're scheduled to pour foundation and there's a heavy rain coming in, it can set the whole project back thousands of dollars, completely wreck my timeline. So I check the weather, I turn off the lamp, and I am out cold. I don't toss and turn. I don't lie there worrying about the mortgage. I don't have insomnia or wake up gasping for air or anything like that. 

The only time my sleep is ever broken, the *only* blip on the radar, is when that urge hits me. If that didn't happen, I'd sleep like a rock straight through until my alarm goes off at 5:30 AM. And the strangest part is, even after I... well, after I go to the kitchen and eat, once I finally go back to bed, I usually fall right back asleep almost instantly. It's like a switch just flips back off. So, no, outside of those trips to the kitchen, my sleep is perfectly normal. Heavy, deep, uninterrupted sleep.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's nighttime eating episodes are related to a sleep disorder
doctor.question: Do you have any history of sleep disorders, such as sleepwalking or restless leg syndrome?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of sleep disorders such as sleepwalking or restless leg syndrome, which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Sleepwalking? No, no, nothing like that. Like I was saying before, when I'm asleep, I am just... I'm out. Dead to the world. I don't wander around the house in my sleep. And Susan, she would absolutely know if I did. I mean, I told you about her ocean wave machine and the Kindle, right? She is such a light sleeper that if I even roll over too heavily, she sighs and shifts around. If I were actually sleepwalking, you know, getting out of bed while unconscious, she'd have had me at a specialist for that years ago. She reads all those medical articles online, remember? She'd probably try to diagnose me herself before we even got to the clinic. 

But no, when I get up and go down the hall to the kitchen, I am wide awake. That's the whole problem, really, I'm totally aware of what I'm doing, just unable to stop it. And restless leg syndrome? No, I don't have that either. I mean, my legs get sore, sure. I'm sixty years old and I spend half my day walking uneven ground on job sites, climbing up and down temporary scaffolding stairs, standing around checking poured concrete... by the time I get home and finally take my boots off, my legs aren't restless, they are just plain exhausted. They want to stay exactly where they are. So, no, I've never had any official sleep problems or anything like that. I don't twitch, I don't walk in my sleep. It's just... just this eating thing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's nighttime eating episodes are related to a sleep disorder
doctor.question: Do you think your nighttime eating episodes might be related to a sleep disorder?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if my nighttime eating is related to a sleep disorder to rule out sleep-related eating disorders. My symptom profile does not contain an item for sleep disorders or their exclusion.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I don't think so. I mean, like I was just saying, I'm completely awake when this happens. It's not like I'm sleepwalking or in some kind of trance. I'm fully conscious. I know exactly what I'm doing. It's just that I can't stop myself. 

If it were a sleep disorder, wouldn't I be, you know, asleep? Or at least half-asleep? But I'm not. I'm standing there in the kitchen, the refrigerator light is glaring in my eyes, and I'm looking at the clock on the microwave, and it says 2:14 AM, and I'm thinking, "What are you doing? You have to be up in three hours. Put the ham back." I'm having a full, rational conversation with myself in my head. I'm just losing the argument. 

And like I told you, Susan is a very light sleeper. If I were thrashing around or doing something weird in my sleep, she'd be the first to know. She'd be dragging me to a sleep clinic by my ear. But she doesn't even know this is happening, because I'm very quiet about it. I slip out of bed, I tiptoe down the hall... you don't do that if you're asleep, right? You don't consciously try not to wake your wife if you're sleepwalking. 

So, no, I really don't think it's a sleep disorder. I think it's... well, I don't know what it is, honestly. That's why I'm here. But it feels like something else entirely. It feels like a compulsion, like a... a drive that just overrides everything else, even though my brain is completely switched on and telling me no. It's just so frustrating, doctor. I've built multi-million dollar structures from the ground up, I manage complex logistics, and I can't manage my own hands in the middle of the night. It's definitely not a sleep issue. It's a control issue. And it's only at night.
